[H1]Introduction[/H1]
Right from the get go, [I]Batman: Arkham Origins[/I] didn’t have it easy. Following the excellent [I]Arkham Asylum[/I] and the superb [I]Arkham City[/I], it wasn’t the sequel that many fans were clamoring for. It was a prequel that nobody expected.

[I]Origins[/I]...a prequel. Not developed by Rocksteady Studios. Not written by the legendary Paul Dini as with [I]Asylum[/I] and [I]City[/I]. Not featuring the iconic Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill to voice Batman and Joker respectively. Just these few points meant this game had an uphill battle to climb in earning fans’ respect. I myself only decided to play this game [URL= https://steamcommunity.com/id/CharlieLima79/recommended/208650/]
after completing [I]Arkham Knight[/I] a few years ago[/URL].

Honestly, [I]Origins[/I] is not a bad game, but it’s also not a great Batman game. Any Batman game at the time that achieved anything less than what [I]Asylum[/I] and [I]City[/I] did was easy target for much criticism, some of which were well founded, some not. I was certainly entertained by [I]Origins[/I] more than I had expected, but I never found myself enthralled by it as I did with its predecessors. That’s because [I]Origins[/I], for better or worse, is a remix of [I]City[/I] with elements of [I]Asylum[/I] thrown in. If you enjoyed the first two [I]Arkham[/I] games, you might enjoy [I]Origins[/I] as well.

[H1]What [I]Origins[/I] Did Well[/H1]
Boss fights with Scarecrow, Killer Croc and Poison Ivy in [I]Asylum[/I], and with Ra’s al Ghul, Mr. Freeze and Clayface in [I]City[/I] were memorable. [I]Origins[/I] also shined in this area despite not having A-list villains to battle. The duel with Deathstroke was intense; the showdown with Firefly was cinematically exciting; the hunt for Deadshot was a predator encounter that gave the assassin his moment to shine after the slightly anticlimactic side mission in [I]City[/I]. Even Batman’s confrontations with Bane accurately portrayed the villain as a smart, somewhat tragic mercenary, rather than simply a mindless hulk that he was in [I]Asylum[/I] and [I]City[/I].

Also credits to Roger Craig Smith and Troy Baker for their respective admirable work in voicing Batman and Joker. It wasn’t easy to fill the shoes of Conroy and Hamill, but for majority of the game, it was hard to tell that different voice actors were used. There were nuances in Conroy and Hamill’s performances that Smith and Baker missed, but they did a great job emulating the original voice actors overall.

And repackaging Riddler’s trophies as Enigma’s extortion file datapacks? Genius.

[H1]What [I]Origins[/I] Could Have Done Better[/H1]
It bugged me slightly that this game is called [I]Arkham Origins[/I]. This game is not a direct origin story of Arkham Asylum. It’s not even the origin story of Batman in the [I]Arkham[/I] game universe. To forcibly work in the word, “Arkham”, into the title for naming continuity sake was silly. [URL= https://steamcommunity.com/id/CharlieLima79/recommended/208650/]
For the record, I also disliked the title [I]Batman: Arkham Knight[/I].[/URL]

[I]Origins[/I] was promoted as a game in which Batman is being hunted by eight deadly assassins hired by Black Mask. It’s a fascinating premise because Batman suddenly becomes the prey, and I wished the developers followed up on this idea fully. At no point during the game I felt like I was being hunted. Also, only six assassins were worked into the main story; you would confront the remaining two only if you triggered their side missions.

The advertised premise, while promising, was merely red herring for the main event. If anything, [I]Origins[/I] is the origin story of the fated antagonism between Batman and Joker. As tiresome as Batman vs. Joker stories are becoming, I thought it was clever of the developers to present us the Joker’s perspective on the relationship, even allowing us to see Batman and possibly the world around him through his eyes.

Yet, there was no equal time spent on understanding Batman’s perception of the Joker and his unpredictable antics. It would have been nice to explore the beginning of their relationship more if this was meant to be the showcase of the game. Still, even the Batman-Joker story ended abruptly, leaving me feeling shortchanged for both story threads.

[H1]What [I]Origins[/I] Did Poorly[/H1]
WB Games Montreal had technical, graphical and design assets from Rocksteady at their disposal when making [I]Origins[/I]. It’s highly probable that the studio was directed to quickly create something to fill the gap between [I]City[/I] and [I]Knight[/I]. This could very likely explain the unpolished state of [I]Origins[/I], even to this day.

Despite having the said assets to work with, WB Games Montreal couldn’t make [I]Origins[/I] look or feel like [I]Asylum[/I] or [I]City[/I] aesthetically. The entire game looked too bright by default. Turning down the brightness couldn’t hide the fact that the exterior environments were drab, as there was hardly any (colourful) accent lighting to make Gotham look menacing. Despite the game taking place on Christmas Eve, Christmas lights and Christmas decorations were far and few in between to make the Gotham look festive.

I also felt [I]Origins[/I] lacked refinement in gameplay, especially with the seemingly haphazardly placed enemies. There would be groups of criminals and corrupt police officers bunched together in streets of Gotham, as well as criminals attacking you the moment you landed on a few Batwing drop-off points from quick travels. There were too many arena battles and not enough predator encounters to provide a balanced Batman experience.

[I]Origins[/I] simply feels just too similar to its predecessors overall, even though it’s not a great imitation. I just wished that given how many ideas and assets were recycled and repurposed for this game, the developers could have incorporated more original ideas. Instead, [I]Origins[/I] has you searching for hidden Anarky tags in lieu of Riddler’s Question Marks; solving similar (if not the same) environment puzzles to unlock file datapacks rather than Riddler’s Trophies; and tracking down Black Mask’s drug stashes and not Bane’s Titan containers. 

Similarly, while I did praise the boss fights, anyone who had played [I]Asylum[/I] and [I]City[/I] would find them familiar. The duel with Deathstroke was a simplified version of that with Ra’s al Ghul from [I]City[/I]; the skirmish with Copperhead also had elements from the Ra’s al Ghul battle; the fight with Firefly was clearly inspired in part by that with Scarecrow from [I]Asylum[/I]. Not that WB Games Montreal did a bad job repurposing ideas, but some new ideas would have been nice.

Finally, given how much of [I]Origins[/I] is recycled material, it’s frustrating and almost unforgiveable that it’s still so buggy to this day. While I thankfully didn’t come across any game-breaking bugs, I often found the game crashing after cutscenes, dialogues and sound effects cutting out, combat takedowns not triggering, and dives not initiating. Within my first 30 minutes of playing, I found myself fighting an invisible boss, who would clip through barriers, in silence. How’s that for first impression?

[H1]Final Thoughts[/H1]
My biggest problem with [I]Origins[/I] is how uninspired it is overall, especially when there were a few great ideas that could have been expanded upon. It didn’t offer anything significantly new that justified it being a full game, when the contents could have been released as a series of DLCs. Yet, because it’s so similar to [I]City[/I], there’s nothing offensive about the content -- only disappointingly unoriginal. I ambivalently recommend [I]Origins[/I], but only to those who want more of what [I]Asylum[/I] and [I]City[/I] offered, and had exhausted those two games completely.

[h1] 💌 Score: [b]7/10[/b] [/h1]

[h1] 👍🏻 Pros [/h1]
✔️ Gotham’s cityscape is immersive and detailed.
✔️ Impressive character design for Batman and his enemies.
✔️ Fun and responsive combat system.
✔️ Engaging gadgets and new mechanics.
✔️ Smooth traversal around Gotham.
✔️ Strong character development for Batman.
✔️ Interesting new villains and familiar faces.
✔️ Excellent voice acting, especially from Troy Baker as the Joker.
✔️ Atmospheric music and sound design.

[h1] 👎🏻 Cons [/h1]
❌ Some textures and animations can feel a bit dated compared to its successors.
❌ More linear than previous Arkham games.
❌ Occasional repetitiveness in enemy encounters.
❌ Story doesn’t reach the emotional depth of previous games.
❌ Some predictable plot twists.
❌ The soundtrack isn’t as memorable as previous entries in the series.

[h1] 🌦️ Introduction [/h1]
Batman: Arkham Origins serves as a prequel to the highly acclaimed Arkham series, exploring a younger, less experienced Batman facing off against a fresh batch of notorious villains. Despite being developed by a different studio, the game successfully captures the essence of what made the original Arkham games so beloved. While it doesn’t quite live up to the high bar set by its predecessors, it still offers an engaging experience for both Batman fans and action game enthusiasts.

[h1] 🖥️ Visuals [/h1]
The visuals in Arkham Origins are solid, presenting a darker and gritty Gotham City that is beautifully rendered. While not as refined as Arkham City, the graphics hold up well with impressive character models and atmospheric environments. The world of Gotham is rich in detail, with lighting and shadow effects enhancing the overall mood.

[h1] 🎮 Gameplay [/h1]
The gameplay is familiar to anyone who has played the Arkham series: a mix of fluid combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving. The freeflow combat system, where Batman takes on groups of enemies in smooth, continuous action, remains as satisfying as ever. However, Arkham Origins introduces some minor tweaks and new mechanics, such as the ability to use new gadgets and counter the occasional boss battles with more complexity. While fun, the game feels slightly more linear than previous installments and doesn’t offer as much freedom.

[h1] 📖 Story [/h1]
The story of Batman: Arkham Origins focuses on a younger, more reckless Batman in his early years of crime-fighting, facing off against Black Mask and other iconic villains. The narrative delves into Batman’s struggle with his identity and the consequences of his actions. While the story is engaging and full of twists, it doesn’t quite have the same emotional weight or depth as Arkham Asylum or Arkham City. However, it’s still a great ride for those who enjoy Batman’s world.

[h1] 🎧 Audio [/h1]
The voice acting in Arkham Origins is solid, with Roger Craig Smith stepping into the role of Batman and Troy Baker delivering an excellent performance as the Joker. The soundtrack complements the atmosphere, providing an orchestral score that enhances key moments, though it doesn’t stand out as much as previous games. The sound design in general helps bring Gotham to life with ambient noise, combat effects, and voice work all contributing to the immersive experience.

[h1] 🥂 Overall [/h1]
Batman: Arkham Origins is a solid addition to the Arkham series, though it doesn’t quite reach the heights of its predecessors. With an engaging story, excellent voice acting, and satisfying gameplay, it’s a worthwhile experience for fans of Batman and action games. While the game does have a few minor bugs and can feel a bit repetitive at times, it’s still a strong entry that provides a solid amount of entertainment. Wait for a sale, but if you’re a fan of Batman, it’s definitely worth a play. The game's flaws are minor compared to its strengths.

[b]When people talk about the Batman: Arkham series, they always mention Asylum, City, and Knight, but Arkham Origins? This game deserves way more love than it gets. In fact, this is one of my favorite Batman Arkham games, and I’ll tell you why.[/b]

[h1]The Birth of the Dark Knight[/h1]
[b]Set years before Arkham Asylum, this game takes us back to Batman’s early crime-fighting days, where Gotham’s criminals still see him as a myth. Warner Bros. Montreal had massive shoes to fill after Rocksteady’s Arkham games, and they absolutely delivered an incredible experience that still holds up today.
The storyline is gripping, focusing on a younger, more ruthless Batman taking on Black Mask, Joker, Bane, and an entire army of assassins on Christmas Eve. Watching Bruce struggle to become the legend we all know was nothing short of brilliant.[/b]

[h1]Gameplay & Atmosphere: Classic Arkham Experience[/h1]
At its core, Arkham Origins keeps the fluid combat, stealth mechanics, and open-world exploration we loved from its predecessors. Gotham is larger, covered in snow, and feels alive in a way that fits the Dark Knight’s early years perfectly.
The boss fights? Some of the best in the series. Deathstroke’s fight alone is legendary, requiring precision and timing, while Bane is a true test of Batman’s strength and strategy.
And let’s not forget the detective mode enhancements, which allowed Batman to reconstruct crime scenes in a way that made you truly feel like The World’s Greatest Detective.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]An incredible origin story: Seeing Batman’s early struggles is captivating.
[*]Top-tier boss fights: Deathstroke, Bane, and Joker are unforgettable.
[*]Expanded detective mechanics: Crime scene investigations were a great addition.
[*]Gotham in winter is stunning: The snowy, atmospheric city adds to the mood.
[*]Classic Arkham gameplay: Smooth combat, stealth, and exploration.
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Some technical issues: Bugs and crashes were common at launch.
[*]No Kevin Conroy or Mark Hamill: Roger Craig Smith and Troy Baker did great, but the original voices were missed by some fans.
[*]Multiplayer mode was unnecessary: A single-player story-driven game didn’t need it.
[/list]
[h1]Conclusion: A Batman Game Worthy of Praise[/h1]
[b]Despite being underrated compared to the Rocksteady Arkham games, Batman: Arkham Origins stands as a fantastic entry in the series. The story, atmosphere, and gameplay make it a must-play for any Batman fan.
This game is a magnificent origin creation by Warner Bros., and it will remain a legend as long as the Batman gaming community lives and keeps loving Batman.[/b]

The best thing about origins in my opinion are the bossfights. Sure the other games have some absolute bangers but also miss the mark sometimes. I don't think Origins has a single bad bossfight. It also has one very funny moment during one bossfight which I am not going to spoil, but let me tell you that the fact that they decided to do what they did in that one specific bossfight shows that they knew they already had an amazing roster and could have afforded it. And guess what? It was pretty good. And also quite funny. And unexpected.

Origins also has a multiplayer option. It's not very good from what I've seen but it doesn't really matter anymore because it was shut down in 2016. What matters is that the achivements are no longer optainable (for those who care) so watch out for that.

There were quite a few DLCs released but honestly only the Cold Cold Heart DLC is worth your time and money.

Overall I see Batman Arkham Origins as the weakest entry in the Arkham series, but still think that it is a really good game. It is worthy of your time even though it doesn't reach such great heights as the main trilogy. To be frank it's quite hard to compare Origins to the rest. It's a black sheep of the series. But one thing is certain, the Batman Arkham series has no bad entries so you can buy any of them and still have a great time.

[h1] ‘On the Shoulders of Giants’ [/h1]

‘Batman: Arkham Origins’ is a taut, immersive, if iterative installment in the legendary ‘Arkham’ series of games – which unfortunately comes in for more criticism than it ultimately deserves. Boasting a strong narrative, an expansive and atmospheric open world, and all the classic gameplay elements from the earlier titles, it is just about everything one might traditionally expect from a sequel. 

[b][u]Campaign:[/u][/b] Released by ‘Warner Brothers | Montreal’ in late-2013, ‘Arkham Origins’ is the third game in a series that revolutionized the super-hero Action-RPG genre and it does not stray from type. A prequel, set five years prior to 2009’s ‘Arkham Asylum’, it features a younger, more vulnerable Bruce Wayne, one still largely unknown to the citizens, criminals and constabulary of Gotham. The opening credits detail a mysterious break-in at Blackgate prison by local crime-boss ‘Black Mask’ who subsequently announces an open bounty of $50 Million dollars for the masked vigilante’s (Batman’s) head, drawing some of the world’s deadliest assassins to Gotham. An engrossing, well crafted campaign of twists and turns will take you across a broodingly atmospheric and expansive, open-world, filled to the brim with side-quests, collectibles, and cold-cases, amongst a veritable who’s-who of criminals, psychopaths and super-villains.

[b][u]Gameplay | Graphics | Sound:[/u][/b] Gameplay is from a third-person perspective, aligned around the game’s 4 main pillars of Flight and Stealth | Combat | Detective Mode | RPG elements (of character upgrades and customization), and these are largely unchanged from the well developed mechanics from earlier entries in the series. Besides the XP-based upgrades to obtain new armor, skills and weapons, a challenge system tasks the gamer with accomplishing targets of scaling difficulty to unlock new takedowns and abilities. ‘Origins’ also introduces two new gameplay features - 1. Crime Scene Investigations and 2. A Multiplayer Component - ‘Crime Scenes’ is an innovative concept triggered at various points during the campaign wherein you are tasked with studying a crime scene, and identifying ballistics, DNA and forensic evidence in an attempt to recreate/solve the incident in a mini-game format. While novel, it is unfortunately somewhat shallow in implementation and thereby predictable, and has to count as a real missed opportunity in driving the series’ gameplay forward. Multiplayer features the ability to play as Batman, Robin, The Joker and Bane as well as various gang-members in a good variety of game modes which while completely serviceable, again seems largely tacked on and unnecessary. Finally, completion of the main campaign unlocks higher difficulty challenges with ‘New Game Plus’ and ‘Worst Nightmare’ modes, and good visuals, strong voice-acting and responsive controls (for both K&M | Controller) round out a well designed, feature-rich offering.

[b][u]Flaws:[/u][/b] Quibbles include average graphics and poor textures in areas, stuttering framerates in others, and a confounding inability to grapple freely onto any surface during flight – a seemingly general lack of the ol’ spit and polish, and a sense that this is more ‘Arkham City v1.5’, than an entirely new game.

Overall, ‘Batman: Arkham Origins’ succeeds in maintaining the legacy of the ‘Arkham’ series by capturing the essence of what it means to be the Dark Knight – be it through brooding atmosphere, an exceptionally strong narrative, a who’s-who cast of villains, a fun and effective combat system, fantastic boss fights, varied gameplay elements and all the toys and gadgets one would expect. Yes, it is iterative and quite similar to ‘Arkham City’, but keep in mind that it stands on the shoulders of two nearly perfect games, and fans of the series should enjoy it thoroughly nonetheless. Generally Well Recommended! – Rated (8.3/10)

[i]Batman: Arkham Origins[/i] is an action-adventure game developed by WB Games Montréal and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment.

[b]Story[/b]
It's a prequel so hey, no need to play previous games!

Arkham Origins is set 8 years before Asylum, with our iconic vigilante being only in second year of his crime stopping career- most of which is focused on beating up ordinary street gangsters and avoiding police.
That changes on a snowy Christmas Eve when group of eight professional assassins plans a hunt on the Bat to earn a 50 million bounty placed by Black Mask, with other villains utilizing this moment to launch schemes of their own; Batman has to stop the killers and prevent criminal plans laid out in Old Gotham.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
Arkham Origins follow same formula as previous two entries, providing third person open world venture where you will investigate, explore, sneak and beat up whoever will require a good shakeup with few changes.

Step up as Batman to plow through your foes with good ol' Freeflow system returning- many enemies (including few new types) and plenty of brawler action await. Attack, counter, dodge, utilise gadgets to chain moves into combinations to create physics-of-law-defying chaos! Be vary of thugs weapons and/or armor, don't get hit to not lose all the build up momentum. Be last man standing to win! This time system comes with tracking of how your combat went and ranking system post fight.

Of course, not everything has to be resolved head on, a good spook will do same work as a fist. In stealth encounters you utilise your arsenal of tools, wits and layout to setup traps, take out enemies one by one and 
enjoy thrill of the hunt as fear strikes into the hearts of common men fighting unordinary. Detective vision will aid in tracking, but once again Bat-repellents- weapons, jammers or mines- will be around the place to make your fun time tad more difficult.

When not dealing with story you can explore snow covered city. Navigate Old Gotham gliding and grappling around to find Riddle collectibles, seek out random activities or tackle side missions ranging from crime scene investigations to fights against stronger villains, including previously mentioned assassins who have a huge hunger for blood money. Another new element here- fast travelling! If you will unlock towers connected to districts that is. Just like before, to reach certain areas you will need a proper gadget you may have not unlocked yet, so be sure to keep "sightseeing-story" ratio fairly balanced. Need a cool down? Batcave is available as a hub where besides plot reasons, you can change outfits or check out training room to tackle on challenges. Right, you can also listen to Alfred's wisdom!

Everything you do- fighting, exploring, collecting- grants you experience points. Collect enough to level up and unlock upgrades, from more armor to improved gadgets. The Dark Knight system adds extra challenges in 4 distinct categories for the best vigilantes who seek to test themselves.

[b]Playtime, replayability, other modes[/b]
Story takes 10-15 hours with extra 5 to 10 spend on side tasks depending on your prowess- giving you roughly 20 hours of Gotham in a single playthrough.

Like in previous titles you can unlock New Game Plus for increased difficulty and newest addition of permadeath mode called I Am The Night. Additionally you still have Challenge Mode (also available from batcave!) where you can grind medals on various maps in both combat and predator encounters.

Extra modes, clean up of open world from collectibles and activites, or simply good combat give a good reason to once again dive into snow buried Gotham if you desire so.

[b]Impressions[/b]
Arkham Origins is good, but doesn't reach level of quality City has going nor is as solid as Asylum.

But first things first. Overall changes in Origins don't "evolve" the gameplay like aforementioned previous entry and are of mixed quality. Fast travel locked behind towers is so 2010's it almost made me shed a nostalgic tear but jest aside, it did provide content and nice Qol feature. Maybe too nice. You will feel that when travelling, as map design is so bizzare and almost forcing you into seat of batjet-whatever it is called- there is plenty of areas that prevent you from grappling or gliding through, plus massive bridge cutting down map in two is diabolical choice to slow the pace down for absolutely no reason. Variety of side missions is pretty good and does hook you into exploring Gotham I won't deny that, once again induldging into fighting lesser known villains and aiding ordinary citizens, even Enigma collectibles mess didn't feel as tiresome as before!

Combat itself still hits for the most part. Fluid, responsive, brutal! With nice scoring system to pat you in the head and inspire to do better next time. Overall balancing is off unfortunately- not even that late in game you get a single tool that nullifies any challenge or tactics of the fights, while most gadgets actually hinders your cause than aid. At some point one has to ask- how many enemy types is enough? Because there were few sections where I felt like game dropped every single variation into a room with no thought what-so-ever, making sometimes for repetitive and long slog to get through. Stealth encounters were a treat just like before, which makes it an even bigger shame that there were so few in story, and none in free-roam! Another weird, questionable choice.

Addition of batcave was nice, outfits look good though none replicate damage our default suit gets throughout the night- and that is the best damn part! Dark Knight system felt just like a cheap reasoning to extend playtime, which with 3 different modes is just unnecessary. Investigations were too simple for my taste and often just a pacing-ruiner, though insight into Batman's thinking process is always appreciated.

Similar to City, game looks great even after all these years and sound design is just top notch, editing, voice acting, soundtrack, you name it!

Now for the somewhat controversial negative- I didn't like the story. It has moments where it does click and few scenes are fantastic, don't get me wrong. But once again we have a rugpull similar to City- attempt to have two main arcs and tie them somewhat together, yet at the end neither felt really fleshed out nor captivated me fully. Entire bounty plot quickly gets side tracked and forgotten while Black Mask...ehhhh. I won't spoiler but I was very disappointed in the way it went. You could have had something great! But someone did the- in my book- lazy choice and I am so worn out on this move game does.

To do a quick summary. Outside of audiovisual side, Origins just doesn't have that something-something fully grasping like previous games had. Combat with new gadgets and enemies is just as enjoyable as before but come with occasional messy bits for no reason. Stealth is great yet there is not enough of encounters to cherish it. Exploration with side content is fun while map layout is annoying. New additions are simply not enough to consider them a change that makes game stand out.
At least setting is nice. I mean, I had my fair share of family Christmas Eve's that did make me want to turn into criminal so ya know, I understand.

[b]Final words and conclusion![/b]
You can take a look at DLC's if you want to further support developers. I can recommend [i]Cold, Cold Heart[/i] content that gives you a small post base game campaign focused on Mr. Freeze.

Batman: Arkham Origins doesn't strike as high as previous instalments but still provides hours of fun brawler combat and solid open world. Can recommend.

There are definitely some similarities between Origins and its predecessors.  The action buttons are almost entirely the same, which was nice since I didn't have to learn an entirely new system.  There is a ton of content, we still have The Riddler as a background story, there are many optional side-quests and distractions, but it felt like there were *too* many distractions in this one.  

In Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, I never lost track of the main storyline, despite my frequent forays into side-quest territory.  Not so with Origins.  I can't count how many times I came back to my computer with absolutely no idea what I was supposed to be doing.  It felt aimless and repetitive, even when I was working towards a side-goal.

One of the things I REALLY enjoyed about the first two games is the riddles we had to figure out.  Oh we still have [i]two hundred[/i] data packs to find (the predecessor to the Riddler trophies we saw in Asylum and City,) but no actual riddles to figure out.  I really missed them, and the data packs simply don't hold enough of my interest to make up for the lack of riddles -- I'm not even going to try to get them all.

The in-game achievements would sometimes work, most times not.  I literally flew from one end of Arkham to the other, and never got the flying achievements.  It took four or five tries to get the notification that I'd taken down two criminals in a slide.  Just frustrating. 

Besides the irritation of not remembering where and what I was supposed to be doing, there was also the frustration of not being able to grapple places that clearly should have been accessible.  It was very obvious where we could and couldn't grapple in the previous games, so I don't feel like it's asking too much for this third game.  We DO have a quick-transportation option, which is nice, but I still would have liked it to be clear where we could and couldn't grapple just by looking.

There *are* some improvements over the first two games.  For instance, when we are locating the "extra special" criminals (those holding information we need, etc) we don't have to save them for last in order to get the information.  If we want to, we can take them out first, then go back and interrogate them when the fight is over.  Another improvement is the crime scene investigation.  They've really added an element of interest to it, although in my opinion, they underutilized it.

Origins is clearly the inferior product game-play and story-wise, but I still recommend it for fans of the series.  It was interesting to see how the back-story emerged, and I'm glad to have played it.  Next time, though, I'll know to skip a lot of the side content and concentrate on the main storyline.  I think that if I do that, I'll enjoy the game much more. :)

Batman: Arkham Origins is the black sheep of the Arkham trilogy — but unfairly so. While it lacks the innovation of Arkham Asylum and the polish of Arkham City, it delivers a surprisingly rich, grounded, and emotionally compelling origin story for the Dark Knight. his game takes place on Christmas Eve, with a younger, angrier Bruce Wayne just two years into his crusade. Gotham is cold, quiet, and full of criminals — and eight deadly assassins have been sent to kill Batman for a $50 million bounty. The setup is simple, but it works. The writing has weight, and the performances — especially Troy Baker as a younger, more psychotic Joker — are top-tier. Combat remains tight and satisfying, following the tried-and-true freeflow system. While not as smooth as in City, it's still incredibly fun. Stealth (predator) sections are just as rewarding. The game also introduces a few new gadgets like the Shock Gloves — maybe a bit OP, but fun nonetheless. The open world is larger than in Arkham City, though sometimes it feels emptier. Still, snowy Gotham is atmospheric, with holiday lights and a heavy, noir vibe. The city feels alive with crime, and the soundtrack adds a haunting, lonely tone that matches Batman’s early struggles. Where Origins really shines is its story. It's not about saving the world — it's about Batman figuring out who he is. His dynamic with Alfred is powerful, and his first encounters with key villains like Joker, Bane, and Deathstroke add real depth. The boss fights are some of the best in the series, especially the one with Deathstroke — fast, intense, and cinematic. Side content is a bit of a mixed bag. There are some fun detective cases and Most Wanted missions, but collectibles (like Enigma datapacks) feel tedious after a while. There’s less polish and variety than in City, but still plenty to do. Arkham Origins is not just a “filler” game — it’s a worthy, character-driven Batman story with great gameplay and atmosphere. If you can look past a few rough edges, you'll find a powerful and underrated entry in the Arkham saga.

I recommend Arkham Origins with a BUT in capital letters: it is a good Arkham game BUT you need to be a big fan of Batman/Arkham games and eager for another hit. Arkham Origins gets a lot of well deserved ire for its flaws. I'll share them with you and then talk up why I enjoyed it anyway.

If you're eyeballing the third Arkham game than I assume you're familiar with the formula by now: simple yet engaging combat, good 3D exploration in a gorgeous open-world environment filled with loving detail related to the long history of the character, a tradition of good spectacle boss fights as established in Arkham City, a comic book plot that hits the right beats for fans and even some decent stealth sections. Tons of content, loads of extra challenge maps, lots to love if you like the series already. 

What sets Origins apart is that it was made by a different developer team. To many Arkham fans Origins is the one that feels off, the one that makes a lot of mistakes, the weakest Arkham. Of the three I've played in depth I would agree. Origins is a 7/10 while Asylum and City dance between the 8 or 9 mark, definitely high end Batman experiences. Perhaps these days we need to take a step back and reflect on what it means for a game to not perform perfectly. Is Origins truly mediocre? Is it really terrible? There are some subtle differences in combat, mostly to timing and whether you can or cannot interrupt some moves. I've got quite a few hours in the first three Arkham games and I can say I got along fine. There's always a bit of a shuffle in the feel of combo flow and counter usage between games and these days Asylum almost looks crude beside City and Origins. All three still play and feel well as far as the punching fellas bit goes. There was never a moment I found myself frustrated in combat by these small differences but maybe that's just me. I'm already used to figuring out the fine differences in how ground takedown works from game to game.

I think Asylum and City beat Origins out on exploration. Origins gives us the largest map but probably the least focus in exploring it. It follows a lot of the good pacing bits City established like the mix of main story flow and the layering of side stories with the traditional Riddler goodies sprinkled about the map. Unfortunately Origins has weaker map design, more empty stretches, more time spent traveling(but a nice fast-travel system to alleviate this so it breaks even I find) and simplistic Riddler goodies. It's not bad but I agree that it is not as good as the other games. But so far we've got a game that lets you fight about as well as City and lets you explore about as well as Asylum and City. For some people Origins will in fact feel better in those departments. So objectively I think the systems are intact and acceptably competent, which is why I opened with the impression that Origins is a perfectly cromulent Arkham game for fans of the series ready for another. Perhaps if you marathon City to Origins back to back you'd be more critical.. I'd certainly be a little tired, at least.

The real tricky bit here is the story. I'd say Asylum has the best overall story for simply going in, getting things done and not deviating. City has a very good comic book plot full of set pieces and fantastic spectacle but falls apart under critical analysis with a potential to zap your enjoyment if you become aware of how oddly everybody is acting. Origins is a strong mid-point between the two I think. The initial plot set-up is great. As a big Batman fan I was champing at the bit with what I was given. Black Mask heading? Eight assassins? A classic night before Christmas Batman plot set-up? Exploring the full city without the flooding of Arkham City i.e. people actually live here? Wonderful! A great innovation in Origins is the detective mode improvements. Before it was almost entirely "Press X to follow the next story beat" but now there's a fun element of recreating a crime scene to look for clues. It's not a huge difference but it's a definite plus.

*Spoilers Follow.* I share disappointment with many players that yet again the Joker has stolen center stage. We get it. He's the biggest villain Batman has, the Arkham staff love him, I love him, this is a prequel story to get around the mess City left us. I'm just very disappointed that the Joker problem(nobody's as big as the Joker, but if you use the Joker every time he becomes dull) is so prevalent and that stronger faith from the writers in the story they had would have enabled Black Mask and Bane to carry the game fully. I can recommend Origins as a strong Bane story to anyone who is a fan of Batman and/or Arkham games, as he's a big star here and his fights and build-up are great. Fighting the rest of the B and C listers is done very well in the main story and the side stories are strong as always, although there's a bit of recycling. *End Spoilers*

Origins is a good game. Origins is a good Arkham game. Origins is not as dynamic and standard-setting as the games that came before it but sometimes all the appeal a sequel needs for established fans is to offer a healthy dose of more of the same. If you enjoy the first two Arkham games than I think Origins will be right up your alley. Just be sure to space out your trips to Gotham as this is more of the same, for better or worse.

I've played through this game once on the Xbox 360 and twice on the PC. It's not bad, and for the price you can get it nowadays... it's worth your time. 

It's basically Batman: Arkham City 1.25, and that's fine. It got green-lit to fill the void between Arkham City (2011) and Arkham Knight (2015), and released in 2013 right smack between the two. Given that it was developed by WB Montreal instead of Rocksteady and existed solely to plug a release gap, it's way better than it has any right to be.

That having been said, it has some warts. 

- There are a goodly number of obnoxious missable achievements. Did you miss a single counter while fighting Deathstroke, but still beat him? No achievement for you and the autosave locks you out of trying again. Did you beat Shiva but take a single hit from one of her henchies? No achievement for you and the autosave locks you out of trying again. I hope you know in advance to manually back-up your save and/or reload each time you make even the slightest mistake, or you're out of luck. 

- The online multiplayer was shut down not more than three years after release, so kiss a goodly number of achievements goodbye. Tough luck. 

- The Dark Knight Challenges are lamentably cruel. Ever wonder why less than 3% of players fully upgraded all gadgets? It's because six gadgets are locked behind these challenges, which need to be done in a very particular order. If you don't do "Worst Nightmare" challenge #6 the first time you visit Gotham Merchant Bank, then you're done progressing down the 15 challenge long Worst Nightmare list. It's over. Give it up. 

If you don't get Worst Nightmare challenges 9 and 10 done in the Gotham Royal Penthouse, then you won't be able to finish all 15 challenges in a single play-through. Tough luck. 

I managed to just barely get it done, with challenge 14 happening at the start of the last level and challenge 15 in the literal last predator/stealth room. It was not fun, but I wanted to finally do it. I can see why it's such a rare achievement.

Also, all Dark Knight Challenge lists need to be done sequentially. So if you do get all the requirements of Worst Nightmare challenge #6 done in the bank, but you were only on challenge #4 of said list... no credit for you. You're done. It's over. 

It's a bad system, and I wish they'd cleaned it up before release to make it less unfriendly. 

___________________________________

But... boohoo, who cares? This game is still a great time, and you can regularly get it on sale for $4.99. At that price, the minor flaws above really feel immaterial. I wholeheartedly recommend it.

Batman: Arkham Origins is a prequel to Arkham Asylum and a sequel to The Land Before Time. 

You play as a younger and less handsome Batman, when he was just starting his career of ILLEGAL vigilantism and his parents were slightly less dead. But still very dead by normal human standards. The game takes place on Christmas eve, a time for celebration and also a time when the diner turns on its heater in the alley and I can be warm at night. A man called Roman Sionis,  Negrodomis aka: the Black Mask and totally the main villain for the entire game has hired several assassins to come make Batman like his parents for the low low price of 50 million Vietnamese Dongs. These villains include Bane, Deathstroke, Deadshot, and several villains you've never actually heard of. 

The combat is much the same as it was the last two games, only with a few more features, such as electric gloves that also double as a nifty way to power your cellphone. Much like a microwave. It also adds a few new enemy types, such as discount Jet Li, and roid-monsters. But old enemies return as well like the random mook, and of course those creatures I am deathly of: girls. 

Stealth is pretty much the same, only this time you also get an upgrade to your spider-man web in the form of a gun that allows you to strap people to gargoyles so you can wrap them up and suck out their juicy goo like the evil man-spider you are. You awful, awful monster. 

The collectible riddler side-mission returns, only this time it reminds me of my high-school years: long and heartbreaking. The riddles and Batman trivia is gone in favor of collecting datapacks that I spent more time doing than I care to admit. There are also these invisible icons left behind by some chump called Anarky, and much like the gay agenda, they are everywhere. 

The game itself is rather jarring compared to the first two Arkham games. While Rocksteady made a rather loving tribute to the Dark Knights in comic and cartoon, Arkham Origins feels much like the movies, taking many assets from the Dark Knight trilogy and clashing themes together much like the skin tone between me and my African twin. Though you can use one of the many skins for Batman after you complete the game, most of them tend to not fit with the theme the game is going for, so you're left out like a DnD nerd at a Fantasy Football meet up. 

The game also gives you the option of playing as Deathstroke in the challenge maps, a character that is rather easy to beat even on the hard difficulty and only shows up maybe twice through the entire thing. And even then, he's just a re-skin of Robin from Arkham City. So you're basically just playing as Robin during his rebellious teenage years. 

This all being said, would I actually recommend Batman's third crusade through the streets of Angsty Metropolis? I guess, if you liked the first two. The side missions are unfulfilling and the Riddler missions make me want to rethink my life choice as a professional street Luchadore. But the game still held my attention for longer than I care to admit, and I still like to look at Bruce's chisled jaw and amazing abs.
That still doesn't make me gay.

Contrary to the public consensus, the black sheep of the Arkham games stands on equal footing with Rocksteady's trilogy. My recollection of Arkham Origins was a bland story wallpapered over an Arkham City clone. While every entry in the primary trilogy does (probably) have a better story, Origins delves further than any of those games into Batman's outlook and his relationship with justice, law, and crime. The game shows us an early-days Batman who has yet to develop any relationship with any of the rogues gallery or classic characters like Jim Gordon. We watch these relationships develop throughout the plot alongside's Batman's approach to crime-fighting during an upheaval in Gotham's criminal underbelly where a new generation of supervillains supplants the mobsters and hustlers of the past. While the Arkham trilogy is about Batman being Batman, this is a story about exploring and questioning what that means. If that sounds at all interesting or you liked Arkham City's gameplay and could go for seconds, then I recommend this game

The basic premise of revisting the exact same setting we got to explore in Arkham City really appealed to me, assuming that I would get a kick out of seeing "Old Gotham" before it was turned into a walled-off prison city. Sadly, it literally never feels like that. Origins' Gotham is visually nearly identical to City's, and is still a de facto wasteland with only cops and criminals running around.
  
- The "Riddler" puzzles are still there (the character is going by Enigma in this one) [i]but[/i] this aspect of the game is [b]severely[/b] simplified both mechanically and in terms of variety/scope.

This baffled me a bit, because Origins is even simpler than the original Arkham Asylum in this regard. Obtaining the datapacks (Origins' equivalent to the Riddler trophies) is much less of a challenge as it rarely requires a clever interaction with the environment or a combination of your skills and tools. One specific tool usually does the job. 
The "scanner riddles" that require you to scan something specific in the environment according to a vague hint by the Riddler don't even exist at all in this game, and even the equivalent to scanning Riddler's question marks, which usually involved precise positioning in order to get the right perspective for the question mark elements to line up, is an extremely simplistic hunt for Anarky's hidden graffiti tags.


- The combat adheres to the mantra "If it ain't broke, don't fix it" [i]but[/i] somehow still feels a little off.

Many reviews have described how certain moves have a tendency to miss their target for no clearly identifiable reason. Sadly, I experienced the same thing. Especially the "Ground Takedown" and "Directed Aerial Attack" are prone to this problem, which is, of course, an annoyance in a game where combos are so important.
I also think that many boss fights overstay their welcome to the point where you've already figured out the intended or optimal strategy/gimmick but it's repeated so many times or dragged out over so many phases that you end up feeling relieved, not accomplished, when they're finally over. 

- The villains and rogues are plentiful [i]but[/i] nowhere near as iconic/interesting as the ones in AC.

Last [b][i]and least[/i][/b] bullet point since this is clearly entirely subjective. Personally, I just didn't care much for characters like The Electrocutioner, Anarky, Firefly or Copperhead. Origins' representations of Bane, the Joker and the Penguin are still quite cool, though.

This may all sound overly negative... [i][b]but[/b][/i] I still had a lot of fun with Arkham Origins. It certainly lacks any kind of unique identity, sometimes even feeling like an AC DLC, however the core "Arkham" gameplay is mostly still there (and in spades; they didn't really cut down on the [i]amount[/i] of extra content, like the combat and predator scenarios, etc.), combat's mostly still satisfying, even helped by the addition of the Shock and Thermal gloves, and the writing is pretty good. I particularly liked this game's rendition of the younger Penguin, and there's some stuff between Alfred & Bruce and The Joker & Batman that's pretty charming. 

As I said, if you've loved Arkham City, then Arkham Origins is likely to at least entertain you as well.

:EDIT:
I have recently played through the entirety of Arkham Knight, and now my respect for the writing in Arkham Origins, especially for the writers' ability to show some damn [b]restraint[/b] when appropriate, has risen tremendously. In a word, the Origins writers knew when to make the characters shut the hell up. The Knight writers absolutely didn't.

Batman has a long history of escaping from some of the deadliest, most elaborate traps a brilliant criminal mind can devise. In his bat-utility belt is a gadget to get him out of nearly any predicament. But in Batman: Arkham Origins, there's one trap Batman can't escape from: the trap of expectations. By now, there are two things that define action in the Arkham series: rhythmic, free-flow combat and stealthy predator rooms. Arkham Origins has those elements in spades. But it doles them out in a straightforward, predictable fashion that lacks the inspiration of the earlier Arkham games.

The most noteworthy difference between Arkham Origins and its predecessors is a significantly larger open world. But that larger world has little meaning when the things you're doing in it are the same things the smaller world of the previous game accommodated perfectly well. Grappling up to rooftops and gliding through the air still feel great, but they don't feel any better here just because you have more rooftops to leap from. And there are side quests that have you doing things like racing to and fro to disarm bombs set by Anarky, which is much like racing to answer Zsasz's ringing phones in Arkham City.

The city is bigger just for the sake of being bigger, and while these side quests make interesting use of characters--Anarky's willingness to go to any length to liberate the downtrodden from the oppression of the rich and powerful makes him a fascinating figure, for instance, and the game gives him his due--the things you're doing are exactly the same as the things the previous game had you doing in its open world. Even the crimes in progress, events you can choose to respond to or ignore that come up on the police radio, aren't a chance to protect hapless citizens of Gotham from criminal elements, but just to fight more groups of thugs, something you do plenty of anyway.

Free-flow combat is unchanged from earlier Arkham games, aside from the fact that there are a few new enemy types in the mix, most notably a martial artist who has an attack you need to counter twice rather than once. The animations are still excellent, and getting into a rhythm where you're dishing out punishment while perfectly countering every enemy attack still feels good, but it also feels exactly the same as ever. At a certain point in the game, you acquire shock gloves that make your punches more powerful, but this doesn't prevent punching dudes in the face from feeling routine.

Predator rooms are also what you'd expect them to be, no less and no more. Of course it's still satisfying to sneak up on a goon and take him down silently, or to be perched on a gargoyle, waiting for a clueless criminal to walk right under you so you can do an inverted takedown. But it's also starting to feel rote. By this point, the mechanics governing these systems have become apparent, the process of sneaking up on enemies or of countering attacks overly familiar. You and Batman and the game he's in are all just going through the motions.
Arkham City built on Arkham Asylum by putting the mechanics in an exciting new context. Arkham Origins lifts them from City and puts them in the same context again, complete with all the same sorts of environmental problem-solving. You still toss grenades into water to form makeshift rafts (glue grenades here, not ice grenades!) and use the batclaw to pull yourself around. You still power up fuse boxes by guiding remote-controlled batarangs through fields of electricity. The occasional encounter with something fresh and exciting could have gone a long way toward making Origins' reliance on these familiar mechanics welcoming. But because nearly everything you do is a straight, wholly unsurprising replication of something you do in the earlier Arkham games, welcome familiarity gives way to an inescapable feeling of predictability.

There is one new mechanic in Origins: a significantly overhauled case file system. As someone who has always been fascinated by the detective facet of Batman's character, I had high hopes that this would make investigating crime scenes an involving process that would test my intellect. Unfortunately, it doesn't. You scan evidence to reconstruct the events of a crime and have to scrub back and forth through the reconstruction to track down more evidence to scan. There's some CSI: Gotham City entertainment value in watching the pieces of the reconstructed crime come together, but your role in the process is minimal.

The one area in which Batman: Arkham Origins delivers occasional flashes of inspiration is in its story, which establishes where Batman's adversarial relationships with the criminals who loom large in the Arkham games began, and how he forged an uneasy alliance with James Gordon, a good cop in a police force plagued by corruption. It dabbles in questions about whether Batman's presence only ends up fueling the fires of criminal activity in Gotham, and in its best and most genuinely surprising moments, explores how Batman and the Joker are two sides of the same coin. As Batman, new voice actor Roger Craig Smith is a bit flat, but as the Joker, Troy Baker fills Mark Hamill's clown shoes admirably.

Batman's eventful Christmas Eve begins, however, with a less outlandish criminal. The organized crime lord Black Mask, tired of the pressure Batman has been putting on his operations for the past few years, puts a bounty on Batman's head, calling eight world-class assassins to Gotham, including the muscle-bound Bane, the poisonous Copperhead, and the efficient Deathstroke. Boss fights with these and other characters have an elevated sense of drama because of the personalities involved, but mechanically, they aren't much different from fights with other enemies. Defeating Deathstroke requires good countering. Against Bane, you use stuns and beatdowns. And so on.

OK, so the game is a mixed bag for me:

Negatives:
1) Graphics are worse than in Arkham City. Hell, they had awesome graphics in E3 demo, what happened?
2) The Joker is once again the main antagonist, and the whole story is revolved around him, with Black Mask becoming a side mission.
3) Shiva and Deadshot are both in side missions, which doesn't make any sense, since they are both assassins. 
4) Some story details are not in line with Arkham continuity, like Harleen Quinzel's beginning. 
5) The combat, while is fine, can break, because Batman decides to push the air every once in a while.
6) Crime in Progress is minimalized to street fights. Furthermore, there are infinite amount of them, which is kinda weird.
7) Some of the gadgets should not be present in this game. Batman's movement is also very free, compared to the future in Arkham Asylum. 
8) They wasted Deathstroke, because he appears after the beginning as a boss, and he is arrested. I feel like he is being replaced by Bane.
9) They shouldn't have made the multiplayer only to shut it down on PC. Because of that, there is no way to collect multiplayer related achivements.
10) Futhermore, if they had focused entirely on single-player, and not the multiplayer, the mobile version and AO Blackgate, the game would have felt much more focused, and looked much better. But WB Montreal/WB Games chose quantity over quality.
11) There are instances, where one playground is used as a mix of combat and predator, which is so bad. Like, they didn't bother. They've got predator snipers and combat thugs on the same tower.
12) Can't unlock the costume "One Million", because I can't log in WBID/WBPlay in game. Someone please, help me out on this one.
13) Because of the way the game is handled, nothing is packaged under one "Complete Edition".  You have to buy everything separately.
14) Missed opportunity: you can't travel to Blackgate Prison. You appear there twice, it would make perfect sense to travel there every once in awhile to visit captured criminals and assassins. Hell, throw some Enigma stuff there too.
15) Some of the "buildings", like Pioneers Bridge and Gotham Royal Hotel have access to the outside. Unfortunately, the game prevents you from going out by flying. You absolutely need to use doors. Same thing if need to go inside.
16) Another missed opportunity. Robin is in the game, yet he is not available in the challenge mode, when he could do so much. 
17) Deathstroke's gameplay is somewhat similar to Robin, which is weird. They could have made him a swordsman with a pistol. Arkham City has a sword swing mechanic. Implement it and upgrade it. Simple as that.
18) Missed opportunity. Why can't we visit the Wonder Tower's upper floors and underground? 
19) The most of NPC's dialogue doesn't have subtitles. Can you guess why?
20) Even though we can talk to Alfred, you can only guess, how many story dialogues you actually have with him.
21) The entire map feels a little condenced. 
22) In trying to complete the Enigma side missions, all you need to do is to destroy the transmitters. You can do so WITHOUT taking over the towers. This allows you to complete this mission earlier than you should.

Positives:
1) The relationship between the Batman and the Joker is very well explored.
2) Bane's story is interesting, with a few twists.
3) A lot of right connections to the Arkham Trilogy. 
4) The mysteries of Gotham is so fun to explore. Cyrus Pinkney's plagues and Anarky symbols reveal so much information.
5) The boss fights are awesome, like Deathstroke, Bane and Deadshot. The latter two are vastly improved.
6) The voice acting is amazing, especially Troy Baker as the Joker.
7) Crime investigation is very much upgraded, although the execution is somewhat minimal.
8) The challenges actually give point to the single-player mode. You might think it's cheating, but this way you gain upgrade points much faster. And trust me, you need these upgrade points.
9) Nice touch: in the New Game+, unlike Arkham City or Arkham Knight, only upgrades are unlocked, but the gadgets will be unlocked during the story progression. It felts so weird to use the Line Launcher in Arkham City, and receive it from Robin as if I never carried it. Story wise it makes sense for Arkham Origins, so the pacing could remain the same.
10) New types of enemies, like martial artists and thungs on venom. There are also big guys with TWO hands, and the same guys in armor.
11) The DLC storylines are very interesting.
12) The atmosphere of the open world in Arkham Origins, for what they attempted, is actually worthwhile. It's not colorful for a reason, because WB wanted to create a true Gotham City vibe.
13) If you are a competionist, I recommend you to buy the Season Pass, instead of buyng everything separately. 
14) Well, it was fun to play Robin when he was available. And only in this game could he do an inverted takedown.
15) Some of the familiar interiors actually look realistic in this game, like the Steel Mill and GCPD.
16) The unlockable costumes look spot on.
17) The ability to visit the Batcave is cool, and talking to Alfred is always nice.
18) The towers are actually needed here, since the map is huge.

I still like the game, but right now it's just not worth it. If you have anything to add here, feel free to comment. Also, how can I access WBID in-game?

A FUCKING AMAZING GAME 9/10

Gameplay: 
      Combat - The Arkham series has the FUCKING BEST combat in any video game, there are so many different enemy types and so many ways to take em down. It takes skill and practice to get good at, but it's rewarding and makes you feel like a FUCKING GOD

      Traversal - You can glide and grapple around the city with your cape and grapple gun. Traversal also does take a slight bit of skill to get to places faster and it is somewhat fun too.

      Stealth - REALLY GOOD stealth gameplay. There are so many amazing ways to sneak up on your enemies such as, grappling between ledges, crawling through vents, or just simply sneaking up behind them. And on top of that there is so many different ways to take them down such as, silent takedown, knockout smash, inverted takedown, vent takedown, ledge takedown, hanging ledge takedown, sonic takedown, ground takedown, slide takedown, glue takedown, and a few more.

      Online Multiplayer - The online multiplayer no-longer works (unless you hack the game files and play it, search it up) but it was fun while it lasted

Story (no spoilers):
      Backstory(NEED TO KNOW) - The main character is Bruce Wayne, When he was a kid his parents were shot and killed in a place called "Crime Alley". Soon after, his butler (Alfred Pennyworth) is selected to be his legal guardian. When Bruce is old enough he travels north to the mountains where he meets a group called "The League of Assassins". The League trains Bruce to become an assassin, but no matter what he will never kill, that is his one rule. The reason Bruce is doing all this is because he is still mourning the loss of his parents, and he wants to act as a defender for those who cannot defend themselves. Eventually he returns to Gotham City to become... BATMAN (because he remembered a time in his childhood when he was swarmed by bats and they lifted him into the sky)
     
      What the story is about - The story takes place just two years after Bruce wayne became Batman on Christmas Eve. He is watching the news when an emergency police broadcast states that the criminal "Black Mask" (a crime boss) is breaking into Blackgate Prison. Batman heads there to try and stop him but is too late. Black Mask kills the warden of the prison and escapes. Batman finds an SD card from a destroyed drone and finds out that Black Mask has hired 8 assassins to kill batman (the assassins being: Bane, Shiva, FIre-Fly, Deadshot, Deathstroke, Electrocutioner, Killer Croc, and CopperHead), but he does not know why. Batman must find out what Black Mask is planning meanwhile dealing with all 8 assassins and the police before the night is over. 
      
      Overall story rating - the story is 10/10. It has an entertaining first mission, then its gets boring for about two hours, then after that you will get addicted. It has a great cast of characters, I especially love Gordon and the main villain. Specifically in this game Batman is really brutal and inexperienced, you can see he's young and acting out of rage instead of his love for Gotham.

Hi all,

Today I'll review the odd duck in the Arkham franchise: Arkham Origins. Odd because of two main reasons: as the title states it's supposed to be a prequel, yet it does not by any means should be labeled as an origin story. It's a prequel, sure, but it never feels that way. Secondly and this is more important: this game is not created by Rocksteady (where all others in the Arkham franchise are) but it's created by WB Games. This is why this odd duck never feels as it should. Don't get me wrong, it's a fantastic game again, but if you played the others you will always have that nagging feeling something is off. 

Still, It's a well deserved 8/10 and as it is the weakest of the franchise, that only tells you how good the entire franchise is!

Origins is a prequel, but it uses all the same gadgets and tactics and combo's as the previous games. This means that, if you played Arkham or Arkham city you can blindly play this too. If you didn't, then the controls are explained along the way, but it's deffinately better if you played one of the first games as the controls are intuïtive like that. The story is about "some villain" putting a bounty on Batman's head of 50 mill dollar and there are 8 assasins hunting on him on christmass night in the city of Gotham. The funny thing is in the beginning nobody ever saw the Batman.
This game brings the old, and also some new: xp is measured by how you take down groups of enemies, how many gadgets you used, if you got hit etc. It's nice, it makes you want to score flawless in each fight. the iconic suit is back, and this is one of the things they got right, the suit is now even cooler then the previous ones. Another new thing is that as of now you'll need an assortment of gadgets to solve puzzels, you will often need 2 or 3 gadgets to progress. Unfortunately you'll only figure that out once you arrived there, which means you may need to do some side missions/challenges first to get the gadgets you need.

So it's great, but it does has some flaws which makes you feel this is not made by Rocksteady.

[h1][u] Con's[/u][/h1]

-Something is off with the graphics, you often have this console-port feeling. I imagine new players will not have this, as the graphics are good, but they don't feel like the rest of the franchise. There is less atmosphere.

- Fights are often clunky, like a bad console port. controls sometimes not reacting or simply bugged, especially the all important counter and ground takedown sometimes bugs out. not often though, so it's not all that important but things like this do not happen in the other titles.

- A lot of running around to win time again. Like all the titles in the franchise you can expect to do the same areas multiple times. A huge bridge seperates Gotham city in two, and early on you will need to cross it multiple times.

- Camera is dodgy sometimes. Not as bad as most other third person games but sometimes it's off. Again, a minor flaw, not a big issue.

- Physics are off in this game. And that is the only one in the franchise. You will often be stuck behind things like small walls, cardboard boxes... Where in other titles you either automatically jump over/on the surroundings, here it's clunky and you need to move around untill the jump actually works. It makes the entire feeling of the game a bad console port and that is a big flaw imho. Especially during Anarky missions where you need to go from point A to point B over the city roofs on a timer.

- During the storyline(s) it is often hard to know where you need to go. This happens when inside big buildings. Very annoying.

- Lighting is weird sometimes, making you fight in detective mode.

- Again way too many riddler trophies...

- Bugs. This is the only title that has bugs, like controls not working, or interrogation not working so you need to restart.

[h1][u] Pro's [/u][/h1]

+ Challenges, in earlier titles the challenges where some form of extending the game after you finished it. But here the xp carries over during story. that means you can do challenges during the storyline(s) and gain xp/gadgets by doing them. Given the fact that there are more gadgets/upgrades then you need, this is very well done! Especially early on you wanna do some challenges to get more upgrades.

+ Gotham atmosphere is back, cold and dark. The city is not oozing with life as in Arkham city though, but the atmosphere is really there again. The typical dark DC feeling.

+ Story is again awesome!!! And as it's a prequel you get to see some villains for the "first" time. It is once again, well created and a masterpiece with some plot twists that make the story even longer and certainly will bring a grin on your face sooner or later. In the very least, you'll get to fight 8 assassins in one night, and that is the VERY least.

+ Long game with lots of things to do. Story itself is long, though it feels short (once more : congrats on achieving this feat in every single title), a lot of side missions will also keep you busy and the option to open some challenge maps whenever you want to get more xp is deffinately a plus! Excellent depth.

+ You don't need to be in detective mode all the time! Which is good as you get to enjoy the atmosphere more.

+ Firefly batlle is EPIC!  Nothing going to spoil more.

+ Fast travel options. Once unlocked you can fast travel across the city, and that is a BIG pro! 

+Extra difficulties and DLC content after the main story. It will expand the game for a short while.

Total: 8/10
Graphics: 8/10
Difficulty : Easy to learn, medium to master (not that easy in expanded difficulties)
Content: 8/10
Price/quality: 8/10
Story: 9/10

Batman: Arkham Origins is often considered to be the worst game in the famed Arkham series, which is true but I don't think it deserves all the hate that it gets.

Having played all the Arkham games, I can confidently say that I love this game as much as I did the others. I kind of look at this game as Arkham City 2.0. It uses the same world map as Arkham City and also most of the game mechanics. It does make little changes to the mechanics to make it seem a little less obvious that it copied the previous game.

This game was released because Rocksteady was taking longer than expected to finish their final game Arkham Knight. So, yes its kind of lackluster when it comes to innovating the series.

But what is not lackluster is the story. Even though it is a shorter story than the other games in the series, it is interesting, fast paced and gripping like the other games. The game does a very good job of setting up the world of Gotham and the upcoming events of the of the other games in the series. 

Tory Baker as the Joker is a highlight. Mark Hamil is the quintessential Joker but I have to argue that Troy Baker comes in a very close second. He is extremley believable as a younger version as Hamil's Joker. We maybe used to Kevin Conroy's calm and collected Batman but Roger Craig Smith does a very good job at portraying a much younger and angrier Batman here. All in all the voice cast is great. 

I played this game after Arkham Knight, which is the ultimate Batman experience. So this game does feel a little empty to me. There are things to do within the world but they all come down to collecting things, destroying things, scanning things and beating up people. This is my one major problem with the game.

The fighting mechanics is as great as always. It's basically the same as Arkham City with almost all the same enemy types, so there's not much to complaint there.

The game is kind of poorly optimised for the PC. I had some frame rate issues here and there during my play through at max settings, so I had to turn some things off.

The graphics is really good and detailed. Since the whole game takes place in Christmas, they did a very good job at showing snow and how it reacts to the environment. The in game cut-scenes (that are not pre-rendered) look a little bad sometimes, especially the character faces.

Now, coming to my overall thoughts of the game. I do not think this game is the worst Batman game ever made. It does a very good job at delivering a strong and compelling story with an incredible cast. The game does feel a lot more emptier than its predecessors and successor, but that's something you will get used to as you play. If you are a fan of the Arkham games, this is a must play. It expands on the lore of the games, sets up the events of the other games and introduces a lot of new things. It may feel slightly disappointing as a mainline title in the Arkham series, but I came for the story and I wasn't disappointed.

I personally loved this game. I felt that it's really underrated, and it has a lot of good things going for it. The story may be slightly, and I mean slightly, weaker than City, but the story is definitely better than Knight's story by a long shot.

As a Batman fan, I thought that Roger Craig Smith did an excellent portrayal at a young, inexperienced version of the Caped Crusader.

Also, the gameplay is decent. Maybe the fighting system is different from City, but it isn't bad, as to say. This game gets a lot of hate for not being by Rocksteady, but I thought that WB Montreal tried their best with this game, and the best part was definitely the boss battles.

The only major problem for me was that I really hoped that the game would actually show Batman's true origins and let you play it out. Yes, I'm aware that there's a DLC called Initiation. I played through it. I felt like we needed more of a story aspect rather than multiple predator and combat missions for Batman's origins. It may be a personal problem, as I'm actually personally a fan of seeing how heroes turned into who they are through their origins, but I just put it here so that you can be informed in case you were expecting to play through Batman's training in the main story, or his origin overall.

If you're a fan of the Caped Crusader, or DC and superheroes overall, definitely get this game. All of the Arkham games have had great portrayals of The Dark Knight, as all the games have shown an actual good understanding of the Batman mythos. I recommend this game.
